ledger.note: 7 September 1904: the Convention of Lhasa. The British reached Lhasa on 3 August 1904 ('to discover that the thirteenth Dalai Lama had fled') and Younghusband had the regent and the Tsongdu sign on 7 September 1904; 'The British mission departed in late September 1904.'

region.text: the Chumbi Valley

ledger.note: September 1904: Britain holds the Chumbi Valley. The 1904 terms had 'the Chumbi Valley to be ceded to Britain until paid'; infobox 'British occupation of Chumbi Valley until 1908 for Chinese payment of indemnities'. The page does not say when the valley was first occupied (the column left Gnathong on 11 December 1903), so the Convention month is used.

region.text: Kham west of the Dri River, Chamdo and the land to the Jinsha

ledger.note: 1905: China sets out to 'reintegrate' Kham. 'Beijing appointed army commander Zhao Erfeng ... to "reintegrate" Kham into China'; 'Zhao was sent in either 1905 or 1908'; 'From 1905, China temporarily took back the control of Tibet as suzerain power'. The page dates neither the fall of Chamdo nor the extent; western Kham is the reading, held until 1918 (Tibet 1912-1951 page).

region.text: the Chumbi Valley

ledger.note: 8 February 1908: Britain leaves the Chumbi Valley. The British 'continued to occupy the Chumbi Valley until 8 February 1908' after the indemnity was paid.

region.text: Lhasa and the surrounding country

ledger.note: 1910: the Qing occupy Lhasa. 'In 1910, the Qing reasserted control over Tibet by occupying Lhasa and deposing the 13th Dalai Lama.'

region.text: Lhasa and the surrounding country

ledger.note: August 1912: Qing forces leave central Tibet. After the Xinhai Lhasa turmoil the Qing officials were 'forced to sign the "Three Point Agreement" for the surrender and expulsion of Qing forces in central Tibet' (infobox 12 August 1912); Tibet under Qing rule page: the amban 'submitted a formal letter of surrender to the Dalai Lama in the summer of 1912'.

region.text: Kham west of the Dri River, Chamdo

ledger.note: 1912: the Qing fall, and Chinese control of western Kham passes to the Republic. The Qing dynasty's end is this event's reason, not the page's statement about Kham; the Tibet 1912-1951 page says only that eastern Kham was governed 'by local princes and then Chinese warlords' and that Lhasa regained Chamdo in 1918.

region.text: Kham west of the Dri River, Chamdo

ledger.note: 1912: Chamdo and western Kham stay in Chinese hands under the Republic until 1918. Tibet (1912-1951) page: 'In 1918, Lhasa regained control of Chamdo and western Kham.' The page names no holder for 1912-1917 and gives no 1912 event for Kham; it also says 'After the 1911 Revolution however, Chinese forces lost ground control beyond the city of Kangding' (a 1940s recollection of the Zhao Erfeng years). That the land was Chinese-held is the reading of the verb 'regained' and of the 1905 occupation (confidence lowered from 2 to 1 in review). The land is drawn as Tibetan under occupation (keyframes 1912-1917), not as lost.

1913: the 13th Dalai Lama proclaims Tibet independent. 'In 1913, the Dalai Lama issued a proclamation'; '"We are a small, religious, and independent nation", the proclamation continued'; 'For the next thirty-six years, Tibet had de facto independence'. The Tibet 1912-1951 page: Declaration of Independence 4 April 1912, Dalai Lama back in Lhasa January 1913, treaty with Mongolia at Urga in January 1913. Recorded as a rename only because no event type fits a change of status: the name and land are unchanged and the Qing protectorate ends.

region.text: the Tawang tract south of the McMahon Line

ledger.note: 3 July 1914: the Simla Convention cedes Tawang on paper. 'The 1914 Simla Accord defined the McMahon Line as the new boundary between British India and Tibet'; 'By this treaty, Tibet relinquished several hundred square miles of its territory, including Tawang, but it was not recognised by China.' Tibet 1912-1951 page: Simla signed 3 July 1914. The British made no move until 1938, so the tract is contested, not lost.

region.text: Chamdo and western Kham

ledger.note: 1918: the Chinese occupation of western Kham ends and Lhasa holds the land again. '1918: Lhasa regained control of Chamdo and western Kham. A truce set the border at the Yangtze River.' Review fix (F4): the 1918 'gain' of the first version is deleted; the land never left the owner's shape (keyframes 1912-1917), so no gain and no earlier loss is booked.

region.text: Chinese-administered eastern Kham (Xikang) and the Yushu region of Qinghai

ledger.note: May-June 1930: the Sino-Tibetan War opens. The war 'began in May and June 1930 when the Tibetan Army under the 13th Dalai Lama invaded' 'the Chinese-administered eastern Kham region (later called Xikang)' and 'the Yushu region in Qinghai'. The page names no town taken in 1930-31 and is silent on Dege, Garze and Xinlong.

region.text: eastern Kham and Yushu, given up behind the Jinsha

ledger.note: 1933: the truces. 'The Tibetans were pushed back to the other side of the Jinsha River'; 'Separate truces were signed by Ma and Liu with the Tibetans in 1933, ending the fighting'; 'All Tibetan (Kham) territories east of the Yangtse fell into Chinese hands, with the Upper Yangtse River becoming the border'. Infobox: 1930-1932, Chinese victory; 'British pressure led Nanjing to declare a ceasefire' (undated). Cliopatria cuts Tibet to 0.91 M km2 in 1932, which the page does not support.

region.text: the Tawang tract south of the Sela Pass

ledger.note: 1944: British India extends its administration into the Tawang tract. 'In 1944, administrative control was extended over the area of the Tawang tract lying South of the Sela Pass'; 'no steps were taken to evict the Tibetan from the area North of the pass which contained Tawang town'. In 1938 Capt. G. S. Lightfoot's column went to Tawang. The tract's position after the Raj ends is not on any page opened.

region.text: the Tawang tract

ledger.note: 1947: the Raj ends (Cliopatria's British Raj row ends in 1947). Page silent on what became of the Tawang claim between 1947 and 1951; the contest is closed here and not reopened with India.

region.text: the Tawang tract south of the Sela Pass

ledger.note: 1947: the Raj ends (Cliopatria's British Raj row ends in 1947). Page silent on the area south of the Sela Pass after 1947.

region.text: Chamdo and western Kham

ledger.note: October 1950: the PLA takes Chamdo. 'the People's Liberation Army (PLA) crossed the Jinsha River on 6 or 7 October 1950'; 'Two PLA units quickly surrounded the outnumbered Tibetan forces and captured the border town of Chamdo by 19 October'; the area was 'placed under the authority of the Qamdo Liberation Committee and outside the Tibetan Government's control'.

region.text: Chamdo and western Kham

ledger.note: 23 May 1951: Chamdo passes into the PRC. 'In 1951, U-Tsang and western Kham's Chamdo area "were annexed by the newly formed People's Republic of China"'.

region.text: Tibet as the Seventeen Point Agreement found it

ledger.note: 23 May 1951: the Seventeen Point Agreement ends Tibet's independence. 'Tibetan representatives in Beijing and the PRC Government signed the Seventeen Point Agreement on 23 May 1951', authorising 'the PLA presence and Central People's Government rule in Political Tibet'; the Dalai Lama's government nonetheless 'remained in place in the areas of Tibet where it had ruled' until 1959 (Ganden Phodrang page: 'dissolved in 1959'). The page does not date the PLA's entry into Lhasa.

wars.name: Gushi Khan's conquest of Tibet

zones.text: Kham, the Beri king's realm, crushed in the winter of 1640-41
Shigatse and the Tsangpa realm, taken in March 1642

wars.outcome: Gushi Khan destroys the Beri king in Kham (winter 1640-41) and the Tsangpa at Shigatse (March 1642); the 5th Dalai Lama is given the temporal power and Tibet becomes a Khoshut protectorate.
wars.note: The Khoshut page gives the winter of 1640-41 for Beri and 1642 for the Tsangpa; the khoshut-khanate dossier starts the campaign in June 1639 from the Gushi Khan page, which was not opened here. Tsangpa page: the 1605-1635 conflicts between the Tsangpa and the Gelug (U invaded in 1605, Lhasa occupied in 1623, an army under prince Arslan in 1635) are the same struggle, not a separate war. Tsangpa page: the campaign starts in 1641 ('In 1641, ... Güshi Khan, set out from his home area') and moves on Tsang only 'after having defeated Beri'.

wars.name: Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal War

zones.text: Ladakh, occupied except Basgo and Tingmosgang

wars.outcome: Treaty of Tingmosgang (1684): the border is fixed at the Lhari stream near Demchok and Guge goes to Tibet; Ladakh reduced to its present borders.
wars.note: The page names the Mughal intervention of 1683 that 'lifted the siege of Basgo' and the Tibetan siege of 'the next three years'. The page speaks of a 'Tibeto-Mongol army' without naming the Mongol side.

wars.name: Dzungar conquest of Tibet

zones.text: Lhasa and Central Tibet, held from 1717 to 1720

wars.outcome: Lha-bzang Khan killed 2 December 1717; Dzungar military government until the Qing expedition under Yunti expelled them in 1720.
wars.note: Infobox: 'Dzungar victory'; 'Brief Dzungar conquest of Tibet until Qing expedition'. The page does not say how far the occupation reached or date the Qing entry into Lhasa.

wars.name: Sino-Nepalese War
wars.outcome: Gorkha invasions of 1788 and 1791 end in the Treaty of Kerung (1789) and the Treaty of Betrawati (2 October 1792); status quo ante bellum, Nepal a Qing tributary.
wars.note: Infobox: 'Status quo antebellum'. The page does not say Kuti and Kerung were retaken in 1792.

wars.name: Sino-Sikh War (Dogra invasion of Tibet)
belligerents: Dogra forces of the Sikh Empire
wars.outcome: The Dogras 'attempted to establish their authority on U-Tsang but were defeated in the Sino-Sikh War (1841-1842)'.
wars.note: One sentence on the Tibet under Qing rule page; no territorial change, so no zone. The war's own page was not opened (page budget); the name is the page's, not an article title.

wars.name: British expedition to Tibet

zones.text: the Chumbi Valley and the road to Gyantse

wars.outcome: Convention of Lhasa (7 September 1904): indemnity, recognition of the Sikkim-Tibet border, the Chumbi Valley held until the indemnity was paid (8 February 1908).
wars.note: Infobox: 'British-Indian victory'; 'Return to status quo ante bellum'; 1906 Anglo-Chinese Convention: Britain agreed 'not to annex Tibetan territory'.

wars.name: Zhao Erfeng's Kham campaign and the Qing occupation of Lhasa

zones.text: Kham west of the Dri River, Chamdo

wars.outcome: Kham 'reintegrated' into China from 1905 (or 1908); Lhasa occupied and the 13th Dalai Lama deposed in 1910; Qing forces surrender in the summer of 1912 (Three Point Agreement, 12 August 1912).
wars.note: The page gives Zhao's dispatch as '1905 or 1908' and calls these events neither a war nor a campaign by an article title; the name is descriptive.

wars.name: Simla Convention and the McMahon Line dispute over Tawang

zones.text: the Tawang tract (Monyul), the 15 Cliopatria cells that the Raj's McMahon Line cuts from Tibet

wars.outcome: No fighting: the 1914 Simla Accord defined the McMahon Line and Tibet 'relinquished several hundred square miles of its territory, including Tawang' on paper, but China did not recognise the treaty; the British sent a small column in 1938 and extended administration south of the Sela Pass in 1944, leaving the Tibetans north of it where Tawang town lies.
wars.note: Added in review (rule 10: the 1914 contest_start belongs to a war's zone). The Tawang district page reports no fighting over Tawang 1914-1947 and says nothing on the years 1947-1951 (it passes to the 1950s annexation and the 1962 war), so the closing year 1947 (the Raj's end) is a confidence-1 bridge, as in the ledger. The name is descriptive, not an article title.

wars.name: Tibetan recovery of Chamdo and western Kham
wars.outcome: 'Lhasa regained control of Chamdo and western Kham. A truce set the border at the Yangtze River.'
wars.note: The page gives only 1918; the start of the fighting is not dated there. The name is descriptive.

wars.name: Sino-Tibetan War
wars.outcome: Chinese victory: the Tibetans are pushed back across the Jinsha and the Upper Yangtze becomes the border; truces of 1933.
wars.note: Infobox 1930-1932; the text dates the truces to 1933 and a ceasefire to British pressure without a date.

wars.name: Battle of Chamdo and the annexation of Tibet

zones.text: Chamdo and western Kham, taken by 19 October 1950

wars.outcome: The PLA crosses the Jinsha on 6-7 October 1950 and takes Chamdo by 19 October; the Seventeen Point Agreement of 23 May 1951 affirms Chinese sovereignty.
wars.note: The page does not date the PLA's entry into Lhasa; the Tibetan government stayed in place to 1959.

certainty.note: The frontier of Ü-Tsang is approximate throughout (Kham is outside the state until 1642, Amdo, Kokonor and the Qaidam Basin always, Guge until 1684, Latö until 1612 and Mangyül Gungthang until 1619; the Ming and Tibetan lines are not dated by any page). The Ladakh border becomes sharp in 1684.
The western border is sharp from the 1684 Treaty of Tingmosgang ('the Lhari stream near Demchok'); the eastern and northern frontiers are soft.

The Dri River frontier was agreed with Beijing in 1726-27 and marked by a stone monument; the Tibet-Qinghai border was demarcated after the Thirteen Articles of 1724 ('the borders between Tibet, Qinghai, Sichuan and Yunnan were demarcated'; History of Tibet). The Himalayan frontier is soft until the Betrawati settlement of 1792 (status quo ante bellum); the Sikkim-Tibet border was recognised in the 1904 Convention of Lhasa.

The Yangtze (Jinsha) frontier was fixed by the 1918 truce and the 1933 truces and the McMahon Line by the 1914 Simla Accord, but China did not recognise the latter and the Ladakh, Xinjiang and Qinghai edges were never surveyed: the frontier is soft except along the Yangtze.

notes: STARTS IN 1354 (Phagmodrupa, infobox 'Established: 1354'), not 1363 as the first Cliopatria shape does; 1354-1362 is a new keyframe that overlaps the Cliopatria Yuan Dynasty row. Tibet, Cliopatria 'Tibet' 1363-1952 (49 shapes), merged into one state from the Phagmodrupa regime of 1354 to the Seventeen Point Agreement of 23 May 1951; the Phagmodrupa, Rinpungpa, Tsangpa and Ganden Phodrang periods are renames of one state, as the Cliopatria row has it. Sixteen pages opened (14 for the budget, 2 more in the review fixes: Karma Phuntsok Namgyal, Mangyul Gungthang); the dossier ledger has 45 events. (1) THE SHAPE BEFORE 1642 (corrected in review, F1/F3): Cliopatria draws the whole plateau (1.55 M km2) for 1363-1641; the pages say the Phagmodrupa 'in the first place wielded power over Central Tibet', that its power was 'reduced to U' by the Rinpungpa and that the Beri king still held Kham in 1640-41. The shapes of 1354-1641 are therefore Ü-Tsang: the gazetteer's Central Tibet (which is the whole Tibet Autonomous Region, 4,342 cells) less Chamdo (the gazetteer's Kham, 699 cells), less the Guge circle (173 cells; annexed 1684), and until their conquest less Latö (113 cells; 1612) and Mangyül Gungthang (59 cells; 1619): 3,298 cells (0.83 M km2) in 1354-1611, 3,411 in 1612-1618, 3,470 (0.88 M km2) in 1619-1641. The Tsangpa page also puts the Tsangpa conquest of Ü in 1618-1620 (Kyishö and Tsal 1618, Nêdong 1620) and gives the eastern 'new acquisitions' (Dagpo, Phanyul, Neu) no date; the drawn shape still holds all of Ü from 1354 (thin; Tsangpa reach 1565-1620 left to the gap-filler). No page opened says who held Kham and Amdo in 1354-1641 (the Ming appointed commissions there on paper); the rendering agent should draw them as nobody's land or leave them to the Ming dossier. From 1642 the shape is Cliopatria's plateau less Kokonor and the Qaidam Basin (the 921 northern cells, the Khoshut home realm: 'the Khoshut realm encompassed Kokonor and the Qaidam Basin while Tibet was a protectorate') and less Guge until 1684; Kham comes in with the 1642 grant of temporal power (ledger 1642, counterpart khoshut-khanate, confidence 2). The Qing province of Qinghai of 1724 is therefore no Tibetan loss and the 1724 loss event of the first version is deleted. The gazetteer needs a separate U-Tsang region (Central Tibet less Chamdo and Ngari); until then the dossier writes it as a minus. (2) STATUS: Tibet was a protectorate of the Khoshut Khanate 1642-1717 and of the Qing 1720-1912 (Ganden Phodrang infobox), a fanbu ('vassal') on the Qing's own terms (Tibet under Qing rule page); this dossier does not record those tints, because vassal events belong to the suzerain's ledger. The khoshut-khanate dossier books Central Tibet as its own gain in 1642 and the dzungar-khanate dossier books it as a gain in 1717; the orchestrator should decide whether those two become vassal_start/vassal_end with counterpart 'tibet' (and the Dzungar side an occupation), or the map will paint Tibet three times. The review (F2) asks for the matching 1642 event in khoshut-khanate: a loss (or transfer) of Kham to 'tibet', since this dossier now books Kham as a 1642 gain from khoshut-khanate; if the orchestrator prefers the protectorate model (Tibet holds the plateau, Kokonor included, under a Khoshut suzerain), khoshut-khanate's 1641/1642 gains become vassal events and tibet_1642-tibet_1721 regain the 921 Kokonor cells. The qing-dynasty dossier should carry vassal_start 1720 / vassal_end 1912 with counterpart 'tibet'. The Ming (1373 tribute, the Guanding Guoshi and Chanhuawang titles, military commissions) and the PRC (1951-1959 protectorate) likewise. (3) TSANGPA: the khoshut-khanate dossier uses counterpart 'tsangpa-dynasty'; there is no such row in Cliopatria and the Tsangpa are part of this state (rename 1565-1642). (4) DARTSEDO: Kangxi 'also annexed Tachienlu in eastern Kham' c. 1693-96 (Tibet under Qing rule page, no year of its own), but Dartsedo (102 E, 30 N) is outside Cliopatria's shape (east edge 100.8 E at that latitude), so no cell or ledger event is booked; Cliopatria's removal of Batang and Litang in 1702 is not supported (they are east of the Dri River and go in 1726-27). (5) GAP 1794-1911: Cliopatria has no Tibet shape; a new keyframe (tibet_1794) keeps the 1775 frontier. The Chumbi Valley (1904-1908), western Kham (1905-1918) and Lhasa (1910-1912) are booked as occupations, from pages that give '1905 or 1908' for Zhao Erfeng and no date for the Qing entry into Chamdo. (6) 1912-1950 SHAPES: the 1932-1949 Cliopatria shapes (0.91 M km2) omit Chamdo and Kham west of the Yangtze, which the Tibet 1912-1951 page gives to Lhasa until October 1950 (infobox area 1,221,600 km2 = Cliopatria's 1928-1931 shape); marked wrong/adjust to the 1928 shape plus the Tawang tract. The 1918-1927 shapes reach 102.8 E, east of the Yangtze, and are cut to the 1928 shape. The 1912-1917 shapes (Ü-Tsang alone in Cliopatria) now carry the same 1928 shape plus the Tawang tract, with Chamdo and western Kham as Chinese-occupied land (review F4, option a): the occupation of 1912-1918 does not shrink the owner's shape and the 1918 'gain' is deleted. The Sino-Tibetan War page says Tibetan-held territory east of the Yangtze fell to China in 1932; the Tibet 1912-1951 page puts the 1918 truce at the Yangtze; the two are not reconciled (booked as a contest 1930-33, no gain). (7) TAWANG: Cliopatria removes the tract in 1914 and restores it in 1939; the Tawang page has Tibetans administering north of the Sela Pass until after 1944; booked as contested from 1914, British-occupied south of the Sela from 1944, both closed at 1947 (page silent on 1947-51). (8) Cliopatria shapes of 1363-1635 differ by 1-12 cells (Ming, Bhutan, Gorkha edges); the edge cells of 1744-1772 and 1947-1948 are unverified: page budget. 1683's 212 added cells are cut to the Tawang tract; 1788/1791/1792 cuts are read as occupations (status quo ante bellum), not cessions. (9) NOT COVERED: the Rinpungpa seat (Nedong is kept to 1564), the Dalai Lamas as a ruler strip after 1642 (no list page opened; rulers only for the Phagmodrupa to 1432 and the Tsangpa), the Panchen Lama's authority over Tsang from 1728, Sikkim and Bhutan frontiers, the 1888 Sikkim expedition, the 1841-42 war beyond one sentence, the Sakya period 1260-1353 (Yuan row). (10) Region names the gazetteer lacks: U-Tsang (Central Tibet less Chamdo and Ngari), Ngari, Guge, Latö (western Tsang: Latö Lho and Latö Chang), Mangyül Gungthang, Tawang, Chumbi Valley, Kuti, Kerung, Tachienlu/Dartsedo (not used), Batang, Litang, Nedong; the dossier uses coordinates (circles for Guge, Latö, Mangyül Gungthang are the author's placements) and the Cliopatria-derived Tawang cells (the difference of the 1939 and 1938 shapes). (11) Confidence 1 events: the 1681 Tawang gain (page dates only the monastery), the 1912 Chinese occupation of western Kham, and the 1947 closing of the Tawang contest and occupation. (12) REVIEW FIXES (ea-06-b-fixed, 2026-10-19), all against the review of ea-06-b: F1 the pre-1642 shapes no longer carry Chamdo and Guge; F2 Kokonor/Qaidam cut from 1642-1726, the 1642 gain restricted to Kham and the plateau fringe with counterpart khoshut-khanate, the 1724 Qinghai loss deleted (disagreement, see below); F3 the 1612 gain re-regioned to western Tsang (Latö) after the Karma Phuntsok Namgyal page, the 1619 Gungthang conquest added, Guge held out of the shape until 1684 (new keyframes tibet_1612, tibet_1619, tibet_1684); F4 option (a): keyframes 1912-1917 carry Chamdo and western Kham, the 1918 gain is deleted, the 1912 occupation start lowered to confidence 1 (the page names no holder); F5 a wars entry for the Simla Convention/McMahon Line dispute over Tawang; F6 the 1641 contest_start cites the Tsangpa page at confidence 2. DIFFERENCES FROM THE REVIEW'S FIXES: (a) F2 asks for the 1642 gain 'intersect with region Kham'; the gain here is Cliopatria's 1642 plateau less Ü-Tsang, Kokonor and Guge, because the name Kham leaves 233 cells of the plateau's fringe in the shape without an event. (b) F4 option (a) asks for the union with Kham x Tibet 1929 (879 cells); keyframes 1912-1917 take the whole 1928 shape (plus Tawang), because Cliopatria's 1918 shape adds 363 further cells at 92-94 E (Nagchu-Biru) that would otherwise enter in 1918 without an event; the occupation events keep the 879-cell Kham region. (c) F1 suggests a three-operand minus; the schema allows two, so the spec is nested. (d) F3: the review leaves 'Ngari Gyelpo = Mangyül Gungthang' to the author; the Karma Phuntsok Namgyal page confirms the 1612-13 expedition to Ngari, where Mangyül Gungthang was subjugated and Latö fell, but names no 'Ngari Gyelpo', 'Lhopa' or 'Changpa' (the Tsangpa page names them without places), so only the Gungthang and Latö readings are drawn; the Gungthang page gives 1620 for its fall, the Tsangpa page 1619 (kept). The review's hint that Ladakh may have held Guge before 1684 is not supported: neither the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal War page nor the Tsangpa page says who held Guge, so no Ladakhi hold is booked. (e) F2's protectorate alternative was not adopted; it is an orchestrator decision (see problems in the report). fx-54 (3 Nov 2026): the December 1717 gain from khoshut-khanate (ledger/18) is the mirror of khoshut-khanate ledger/10; the Dzungar side is an occupation_start with counterpart tibet (dzungar-khanate ledger/15), so Tibet is the owner of hatched land in 1717-1720.
